The art of video editing is an intricate process that involves a multitude of
complex decisions made by skilled editors. This process is characterized by
their exceptional expertise, which is difficult to replicate. To bridge this
gap, researchers are working on developing artificial intelligence (AI) systems
that can assist editors by automating routine tasks and providing expert-level
guidance. However, the effectiveness of these AI systems relies heavily on
having extensive datasets of professional editing decisions. This paper

collected from over 100 edited videos. These videos were analyzed to identify
the various editing operations performed, including cut points, transitions, and
visual effects. This dataset is then used to create a benchmark suite for AI
researchers to develop more accurate video editing systems. This benchmark
includes a range of tasks, such as predicting cut points, editing boundaries,

video editing and provide a foundation for future research in the field. The
dataset and benchmark are available for public access at

In offline reinforcement learning, we tackle the challenge of policy optimization with fixed data, seeking to develop a policy that maximizes expected return. This problem is particularly demanding due to its inherent complexity, which becomes increasingly problematic as the number of states grows. To address this complexity, we introduce a new class of offline reinforcement learning algorithms that leverage a limited number of samples. This approach leads to two significant breakthroughs: we demonstrate that these algorithms can achieve near-optimal performance under specific conditions and provide a framework for analyzing their convergence rates. Furthermore, we show that by combining our method with a first-order optimization technique, we can create an efficient and reliable policy optimization approach. This approach is supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. Our work represents the first comprehensive analysis of offline reinforcement learning using a limited number of samples, providing a foundation for future research in this area. This study presents a comprehensive framework for extracting and classifying
narrative descriptions from diverse contexts, including films, books, and cultural
accounts. The proposed approach integrates multiple levels of linguistic and semantic
analysis to identify key narrative elements. To this end, we employ a hybrid method
combining statistical analysis and natural language processing to classify narrative
types based on extracted features. The framework is applied to the task of
automatically classifying movie synopses from the MovieLens dataset. The results
demonstrate the framework's ability to achieve high accuracy rates, including
F-measures of 0.59, 0.60, and 0.62 for three distinct classification categories.
Furthermore, we demonstrate the framework's capacity for narrative analysis and
identification of story structure components, including setting, characters, and events. 
The framework's performance is also compared to existing classification methods. The
framework's source code is available for public access. This research contributes to
the development of a universal framework for narrative analysis and classification. 
The framework's potential for automatic narrative classification and its capacity for
cultural data analysis are also discussed. 
The framework's source code is available at https://github.com/krishnrajn/narrative.krishnraj.n.

In imitation learning, the goal is to acquire a policy that mimics expert behavior. However, the expert's policy is unknown, making it difficult to obtain expert trajectories. As a result, the learning process relies on offline data collected independently by humans. However, the collected data often lacks mimicry quality, causing the learned policy to perform poorly. To address this issue, we introduce a novel imitation learning method, SoftDICE, which combines the benefits of both behavioral cloning and adversarial approaches. Unlike existing methods, SoftDICE uses a unique loss function that balances imitation and exploration, leading to more stable learning outcomes. We provide theoretical insights into SoftDICE's effectiveness and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods on various benchmark tasks. Notably, the learned policy achieved perfect mimicry in all experiments. We also showcase SoftDICE's performance on a challenging continuous control task, where it outperforms other methods. The code for SoftDICE is available at https://github.com/ekn/softdice. We believe that SoftDICE offers a more robust and efficient approach to imitation learning. The properties of the resulting supersymmetric sequence are explored, including the conserved quantities and the long-time behavior of the solutions. We introduce a novel method for refining a digital circuit design based on the outcomes of a static code analysis. The code analysis is conducted by compiling the circuit design into a Boolean SAT problem, which is then solved to identify areas for improvement. Once the unsatisfiable areas are pinpointed, we utilize a circuit optimization approach to modify the circuit and create a new design that satisfies the specified constraints. This optimization process is repeated until the entire circuit is improved, at which point we reframe the optimization problem as a SAT instance and apply it to further enhance the circuit design. This iterative process enables us to effectively tackle complex circuits of significant size, resulting in improved performance and reduced power consumption. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods in optimizing the performance of RISC-V circuits, achieving an average increase of 2.5% in clock cycle rate and 2.3% in power reduction. This paper presents a novel approach to evaluating the effectiveness of base and detail image decomposition methods in various visual and computational metrics. To address limitations of existing methods, our approach focuses on two key improvements: (1) measuring distortions in the base and detail components, rather than the reconstructed image; (2) using a range of distortions, not just over- and under-sharpening. We propose a set of metrics that quantify anomalies in the base and detail images, and evaluate them using both subjective and objective assessments. Our results show that the best decomposition methods are highly dependent on the specific image content and usage. To address this, we introduce a new rank-order correlation coefficient that can evaluate the performance of these methods in various scenarios. We demonstrate that this coefficient is highly correlated with the subjective quality ratings of human observers. Our approach provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the performance of base and detail decomposition methods in a wide range of applications. Our proposed training procedure, a hybrid approach combining online and offline stages, enables agents to adapt to novel environments and tasks. To enhance the robustness of neural networks against malicious inputs, researchers employ adversarial training, a method that involves training the network on artificially generated, nearly indistinguishable examples designed to fool the network. However, the effectiveness of this approach is limited by the availability of high-quality adversarial examples. Recent studies have shown that the most challenging, or most effective, attacks on a network are those that push the network's decision boundary to its farthest point. Building on this insight, we propose a novel adversarial training method that uses a reinforcement learning approach to find the most challenging attacks. Our method, Ladder, trains a generator to produce adversarial examples that extend the network's decision boundary, and a discriminator to ensure the generated examples are indistinguishable from genuine ones. By maximizing the distance between the network's predictions and a target decision boundary, Ladder finds more potent attacks than traditional methods like PGD, leading to significantly improved robustness against both seen and unseen attacks. Our method outperforms existing approaches on multiple datasets and models, and our code is available on GitHub. Ladder can be seen as a general framework for generating the most effective attacks, and we demonstrate its versatility by applying it to other decision boundary manipulation tasks. Our method is the first to achieve this. Our findings are accompanied by a video showcasing the improved robustness of Ladder-trained models against malicious inputs. The task of bird species classification is a complex image recognition problem 
that has been a benchmark for computer vision research. This study presents a 
novel approach to categorize bird types, capitalizing on the extensive dataset 
of the Bird Kingdom, which comprises over 5,000 bird types. This research 
delves into the feasibility of applying convolutional neural networks (CNNs) 
and leveraging transfer learning to tackle the challenge. Given the vast 
number of bird species, the research team encountered difficulties in obtaining 
a comprehensive dataset for training. This led to the development of a 
multistage training approach, which involves training a model on a smaller 
subset, then fine-tuning it on a larger dataset, and repeating the process. 
Additionally, the team explored various techniques for transfer learning, 
utilizing pre-trained ImageNet models and custom datasets to train new models. 
The results of this research demonstrate the effectiveness of the multistage 
training approach and highlight the importance of a balanced dataset in 
achieving optimal results. This study also underscores the need for a more 
robust multistage training approach, which can be further optimized by combining 
the methods employed. The research team aims to enhance the current approach by 
further refining the multistage training and incorporating more efficient data 
augmentation techniques to improve the accuracy of bird species classification. 
This research is a significant step towards automating bird species identification, 
which is crucial for conservation efforts and wildlife research. The findings of 
this study will be made available through a GitHub repository, and the research 
team is open to collaboration and further development.

This research introduces a hierarchical control system for quadruped robots that efficiently navigates various terrain and load conditions. The proposed control system consists of two layers: a high-level module that determines optimal control parameters, and a low-level module that executes velocity control using these parameters. The high-level module employs an adaptive control strategy to identify the most effective parameters, while the low-level module utilizes a quadratic programming algorithm to meet motion constraints. The adaptive control parameters are adjusted based on the robot's performance, measured by a cost function combining position, orientation, and joint path errors. The proposed controller's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments on the Cassie robot, showcasing its ability to handle different terrain and wheeled obstacles. The hierarchical control system's adaptability and efficiency are highlighted by its successful operation with minimal prior knowledge of the environment and maximum load capacity. This study explores the potential of using machine learning techniques to analyze the dark matter content of various particle physics models. Specifically, we examine the prospects of models featuring scalar, vector, and fermionic particles as dark matter candidates, each interacting with a singlet fermion particle. By employing a random forest classifier, we can distinguish between scenarios with and without dark matter in the final state, leveraging event information such as mass distributions, kinematic properties, and particle flight paths. Our analysis demonstrates that certain events can be confidently identified as not containing dark matter, while the classification of the remaining scenarios depends on the available information and the LHC's energy level. For instance, when considering dark matter mass and the scalar mediator mass, we can accurately identify more than 80% of the non-dark matter scenarios across a wide range of energies. However, when the dark matter and mediator masses are unknown, the classification accuracy drops to around 50%. In ensemble Q-learning, a well-known method for estimating value functions, a group of value functions with diverse characteristics are combined together. However, a major issue arises when the ensemble's value functions deteriorate over time, causing its performance to decrease. To address this issue, a new approach called VOQ is proposed, focusing on maintaining representation diversity within the ensemble. VOQ achieves this by introducing a unique regularization term that encourages each value function to occupy its own niche in the representation space. As a result, VOQ effectively prevents the deterioration of the ensemble's value functions, ultimately leading to improved performance. Moreover, VOQ's performance surpasses that of other methods, including Q-learning and ensemble Q-learning, in a range of experiments. Notably, VOQ's benefits are not limited to ensemble Q-learning, as it can be applied to any learning algorithm that estimates value functions. To demonstrate this, VOQ is integrated with TD learning, resulting in a new algorithm called TD with Optimized Representation Variety, or TDOR. Experimental results show that TDOR significantly outperforms TD learning in a variety of scenarios. Overall, VOQ's ability to maintain representation diversity within ensembles of value functions is a valuable tool that can be applied to any value function estimator. In the context of differentially private synthetic data, we investigate whether adjusting for sensitive variables through noisy perturbation can enhance privacy. However, previous research has yielded inconsistent results, and the impact of noise in perturbation mechanisms has been particularly challenging to quantify. To address this, we developed a novel inference method grounded in the Bayesian framework, which allows for the joint estimation of an attribute of interest and the removal of confounding variables. This method, termed noisy adjusment inference, enables us to accurately quantify the noise introduced by perturbation mechanisms, and we found that the noise introduced by perturbation mechanisms can be expressed as a lower bound of the mutual information between the sensitive attribute and the perturbed data. Consequently, we found that the optimal noise distribution in perturbation mechanisms can be expressed as a maximum of a mutual information lower bound, and we derived a computationally efficient algorithm to achieve this optimal noise distribution. Our theoretical findings were validated through numerical experiments. This work has significant implications for the design of differentially private synthetic data, and we hope that it will facilitate further research in this area. Overall, our approach provides a powerful new tool for understanding and predicting the complex dynamics of real-world networks. The success of this strategy relies heavily on efficient monitoring and surveillance systems that can track the carbon sequestration process. The development of 4D seismic imaging technology has significantly enhanced monitoring capabilities, but its effectiveness is hindered by the need for repeated surveys, which are often prohibitively expensive. In this study, a novel approach is presented that leverages deep learning techniques to generate accurate 4D seismic images from a single survey, using a spatio-temporal Convolutional Neural Network. The network's architecture is designed to capture temporal patterns in seismic data, enabling it to predict future surveys from a single survey, thereby reducing costs and minimizing the need for frequent surveys, which is crucial for effective carbon storage monitoring. We propose an approach to learn the decision-making criteria of simple neural networks through meta-learning, using data from two distinct tasks. This method is based on the idea of learning-to-learn and is applicable to various neural network architectures. By leveraging this approach, we can derive a set of rules that define a neural network's decision-making processes, enabling the identification of inductive biases and potential flaws. Furthermore, our meta-learning method can be integrated with existing techniques, such as rule distillation and rule-based pruning, to create novel algorithms for training neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving the accuracy of neural networks trained with these algorithms. Additionally, our method provides a means to interpret the decisions made by these networks, revealing their inductive biases and potential limitations. By applying our approach to the task of classifying handwritten digits, we can derive a set of rules that define the decision-making processes of neural networks, ultimately enabling the identification of inductive biases and potential flaws. This, in turn, can inform the development of more accurate and reliable neural networks. Overall, our meta-learning method provides a powerful tool for understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks and improving their accuracy. The ability of humans to track moving objects is a fundamental aspect of their visual perception, which has been successfully replicated in various computer vision applications.  In contrast to static visual following tasks, where objects remain stationary, visual tracking involves dynamic following, which requires tracking moving objects.  This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic following, which employs a two-stage learning framework.  The first stage utilizes a generative adversarial network to generate a stable and clear image of the target, while the second stage is a static following network that focuses on predicting the target's movement.  By combining these stages, the proposed model is able to accurately track fast-moving objects, achieving superior results compared to existing methods on benchmark datasets. However, this hierarchical approach can be inefficient, requiring designers to specify every parameter and resulting in suboptimal designs with conflicting requirements. To address this issue, we propose a novel conception stage that allows users to focus on the overall aesthetic of their desired design, rather than individual parameters. By leveraging natural language processing techniques, our system can interpret these inputs and automatically generate design specifications that meet the desired appearance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through user studies and real-world applications, showing that it can produce designs with the intended look using both automated and collaborative methods. Compared to traditional methods, our system achieves comparable results with fewer user inputs and reduced design conflicts. We also identify areas for future research that take into account the inherent trade-offs between design quality, conflict rates, and user input requirements. Our work paves the way for more intuitive and efficient generative design tools that minimize user input and maximize design quality. Deep learning models have been compromised by backdoor attacks, which can be exploited to compromise security and infringe on user privacy. These attacks manipulate model training to recognize a trigger instead of the target, and can be executed in various ways, including through malicious data injection or model fine-tuning. Once a backdoor is embedded, an adversary can manipulate face recognition systems to misidentify individuals, and potentially pilfer sensitive information such as identity, demographic data, and biometric information. To counter this threat, we propose a novel approach that leverages the strengths of self-supervised learning and self-attention to develop a robust face recognition system that is impervious to backdoor attacks. Our proposed method, which is based on the concept of contrastive learning, can be seamlessly integrated into existing face recognition architectures, and has been shown to significantly enhance the resilience of these systems against backdoor attacks. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the LFW, FGNET, and CALFW datasets demonstrate that our proposed method can achieve substantial performance gains, including up to 90% and 99% reductions in attack success rates, and 10% and 5% reductions in the Equal Error Rate (EER). Moreover, our method can be applied to both training and testing phases, and can be easily adapted to other types of attacks, such as adversarial attacks. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub. Our findings suggest that our method can be effectively employed to develop robust face recognition systems that are resilient to various types of attacks. Our research has significant implications for the development of facial identification technologies, and can be potentially extended to other biometric modalities. In this study, we investigate a complex contextual multi-armed bandit problem where the goal is to optimize a reward function by selecting the best option among N available choices, whose values depend on both the context and the chosen option. We assume a setting where the values of the alternatives are partially ordered, allowing us to develop a contextual bandit algorithm that exploits this structure. We demonstrate that our approach achieves a regret of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ under certain conditions and show that this is the best achievable rate for this problem. We also provide empirical evidence showing that our method outperforms existing algorithms in this context. Moreover, we adapt our approach to a more challenging scenario involving N options and K possible orders, for which we establish a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\log^2 T})$. We also present experimental results that support the effectiveness of our approach in this setting. The source code for our bandit algorithm is available online. Furthermore, we develop a general framework for addressing multi-armed bandit problems with partial orders and demonstrate its applicability in various real-world scenarios. We also identify additional applications of our approach in the context of recommendation systems. We introduce FlexMatch, a novel approach to semi-supervised learning that leverages a curriculum-based strategy to optimize the process of pseudo-labeling, typically used in SSL methods. FlexMatch employs a two-stage framework where initial pseudo-labeling is done using high-quality labels, followed by a refinement stage using cheap, unreliable labels, each with its own unique pseudo-labeling approach. The key innovation lies in the dynamic pseudo-labeling module, which adjusts the quality of pseudo-labels in real-time, assigning more reliable labels to samples with high quality pseudo-labels and bypassing those with low quality labels. This approach is coupled with a novel loss function, the FlexMatch Loss, which combines the losses from both supervised and unsupervised data, and is optimized using a multi-task learning framework. The efficacy of FlexMatch is demonstrated through experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and ImageNet-R, resulting in state-of-the-art performance. VBR is an edition-based memory reclamation method, where each page of memory is treated as a series of versions, each representing a specific memory state at a particular point in time. The technique handles memory reclamation using a lock-free protocol that ensures each version is read through a sequential lock. Upon program termination, VBR performs a post-mortem garbage collection to reclaim memory. The evaluation of VBR on a range of lock-free data structures and workloads reveals significant performance improvements, outperforming existing memory reclamation methods in both memory efficiency and speed. This study focuses on the minimal frequency observations of a diffusion's state, 
which are recorded at times determined by the square root of the observation interval. 
The goal is to develop a general method for deriving the minimal sufficient statistics 
and providing consistent estimators based on these observations. 
The proposed approach is founded on the application of the spectral expansion of the infinitesimal generator of the diffusion process. 
The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to the diffusion of a stock price modelled by the Black-Scholes equation. 
The findings show that the minimal sufficient statistics for the model's parameters can be obtained by solving a partial differential equation. 
Furthermore, the minimal sufficient statistics can be estimated consistently using the observed stock prices at times determined by the square root of the observation interval. 
The study also derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimators under certain conditions. 
The results are further verified through numerical simulations, which demonstrate the practicality of the method. 
The method's applicability extends to various financial models, including those for interest rates, foreign exchange rates, and real estate prices. 
The study concludes by highlighting the potential for further research in this area.

We investigate the potential of deep learning models to automatically correct incomplete 3D surface scans of moving objects, focusing on the impact of motion on both traditional and generative learning techniques. The proposed metric is shown to be a reliable measure of visual reconstruction accuracy. The research also highlights the limitations of current 3D reconstruction techniques in handling dynamic scenes and identifies potential avenues for future investigation. The JSON Metrics Evaluator is a tool designed to assess JSON data quality, facilitating its reuse by rating its quality and identifying potential utilization. This evaluation tool categorizes JSON data into three types: document, array, and value, and contains six key features that evaluate its quality, including compactness, regularity, symmetry, order, completeness, and accessibility. This evaluation tool can be accessed via a REST API or integrated into a web application via a JavaScript library, facilitating seamless JSON data management. We revisit the non-relativistic limit of string theory by re-examining the relativistic string action within a novel non-relativistic string framework. This approach yields a string action that remains canonical, even in scenarios involving soft strings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the soft-string sector can be described within light-cone coordinates, where the relativistic string action is reformulated in a uniform gauge. This novel formulation is then applied to calculate the leading-order contribution to the binding energy of a bosonic string, resulting in a value equivalent to that derived from the Polyakov string tension. Additionally, we extend our analysis to soft strings comprising N Polyakov strings, and also investigate the properties of soft strings within the context of the relativistic string action's non-relativistic limit. This dual approach is then applied to calculate the binding energy of a bosonic string, as well as that of a rotating string. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the study of dark matter and dark energy. Our work also includes a comprehensive review of the relevant literature and the identification of potential research avenues for the future. Hyperspectral images are highly susceptible to noise, a problem that has been addressed by various denoising algorithms in recent years. These algorithms can be broadly classified into two categories: those that utilize prior knowledge of image statistics and those that employ spatial-spectral relationships. This study proposes a novel framework, SSCAN, which integrates both perspectives to develop a more effective denoising algorithm. The proposed framework consists of two key components: a cross-domain attention module and a cross-domain fusion module. The first module leverages the spatial-spectral relationship to enhance performance in the spectral domain, while the second module utilizes the attention mechanism to integrate information across domains. The SSCAN framework is then applied to various hyperspectral image denoising tasks, yielding promising results. To enhance neural network inference on servers, we introduce ENOS, an innovative system that integrates with existing infrastructure. ENOS identifies the most energy-efficient kernels and loads the necessary neural network models from a hybrid memory and software booster stack, thereby reducing energy consumption and latency. Our evaluation, involving real-world and synthetic benchmarks, demonstrates that ENOS outperforms the state-of-the-art by 1.2-1.4 times in terms of energy efficiency and 1.1-1.3 times in terms of execution time. ENOS achieves these results while maintaining a low overhead of 0.5-1.5% in terms of memory and CPU usage. The system's adaptability and efficiency are further highlighted by its ability to handle diverse workload mixes and various memory configurations. Our work is the first to investigate the potential of ENOS in reducing energy consumption and latency across different neural network applications, including those in computer vision, natural language processing, and recommendation systems. To improve the network's performance, we incorporate a self-attention module that captures long-range dependencies between images, and a residual connection that enables the network to learn complex registration functions. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. A positive real number $t$ is said to have the (q, m) property if it can be expressed as $t = q/m$ where $q$ and $m$ are relatively prime and $m$ is a multiple of $4$ while $1 \leq i \le m$. The set of such numbers with this property is denoted by $S_{q, m}(t)$. This paper investigates the properties of the collection of all real numbers with a certain range of $t$ values, specifically those between $0$ and $1$, under the assumption that each of these numbers belongs to one and only one set among $S_{q, m}(t)$. It is found that this collection forms a fractal set and the Hausdorff dimension of this set is precisely $\log(4)/2\log(e)$. Furthermore, the paper also examines the fractal sets that result from combining the collections of real numbers with the ($q, m$) property and those with the ($q', m'$) property, specifically when $q$ and $q'$ are $2$ and $m$ and $m'$ are $3$ respectively. It is found that this combined set is also a fractal set and the Hausdorff dimension of this set is precisely $\log(6)/2\log(e)$. The conventional wisdom in machine learning suggests that balancing precision and robustness in classification tasks often requires a compromise. These findings challenge the long-held assumption that a robot must sacrifice precision for robustness in complex real-world environments. Instead, we propose that a robot's performance in such settings can be improved by prioritizing the development of high-precision interaction skills. The results of this study have significant implications for the design of future interactive robots working in dynamic, real-world settings. The OR-Expense model is adaptable to various light field cameras and can be implemented using a wide range of depth assessment metrics. The system's low computational requirements enable efficient deployment on embedded platforms, making it suitable for real-time use.
